summary: Nahum 3 opens with a woe against the “bloody city,” then rushes through battle noise, bodies, and public disgrace. The chapter compares Nineveh with No-Amon, whose defenses and allies did not keep it from captivity. It ends by portraying Nineveh’s defenses, merchants, officials, shepherds, and king as unable to prevent a fatal wound.
whyItMatters: This final chapter brings the book’s accusation against Nineveh to its sharpest point: violence, deception, and predatory power return on the city. It also leaves readers with the book’s tension, since relief from cruelty is described through severe images of war and humiliation.

context.author: The heading of the book attributes the vision to Nahum the Elkoshite, but gives no biography and does not identify who arranged the book in its final form.
context.audience: Judah is directly addressed elsewhere in the book with news of relief, while Nineveh and Assyrian power are the main targets of the poems.
context.date: Commonly oriented between the Assyrian sack of Thebes in 663 BCE, recalled as past, and Nineveh’s fall in 612 BCE, portrayed in the poetry; the book itself gives no exact date.
context.setting: The seventh-century BCE world of Assyria and Judah, with Nineveh as the Assyrian capital and No-Amon recalled as a comparison.
context.literaryForm: Prophetic poetry using accusation, battle imagery, taunt, direct divine speech, commands, questions, and a final address to Assyria’s king.

outline.heading: Woe over a violent city
outline.note: Nineveh is accused as a city full of bloodshed, lies, robbery, battle, corpses, prostitution, and witchcraft that ensnare nations and families.

outline.heading: Public shame and abandonment
outline.note: Yahweh speaks directly against the city, threatening exposure, filth, spectacle, flight, and the absence of mourners or comforters.

outline.heading: No-Amon as a warning
outline.note: The poem asks whether Nineveh is stronger than No-Amon, then recalls that city’s allies, captivity, murdered children, enslaved leaders, and defeat.

outline.heading: Defenses that fail
outline.note: Fortresses are compared to ripe figs, gates stand open, and the city is told to prepare for siege though fire and sword will still devour it.

outline.heading: Locust-like abundance and flight
outline.note: Merchants, guards, and officials are compared to grasshoppers and locust swarms that multiply, settle briefly, and disappear.

outline.heading: The king’s fatal wound
outline.note: The king of Assyria is addressed as shepherds and nobles fail, the people scatter, and hearers clap because of Assyria’s endless cruelty.

keyVerses.text: Woe to the bloody city! It is all full of lies and robbery—no end to the prey.
keyVerses.why: This line states the chapter’s central accusation against Nineveh: bloodshed, deception, robbery, and predatory gain.

keyVerses.text: “Behold, I am against you,” says Yahweh of Armies, “and I will lift your skirts over your face. I will show the nations your nakedness, and the kingdoms your shame.
keyVerses.why: The divine speech formula marks a direct judgment against the personified city, using violent exposure imagery that readers need to name carefully.

keyVerses.text: Are you better than No-Amon, who was situated among the rivers, who had the waters around her, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was of the sea?
keyVerses.why: The comparison with No-Amon challenges Nineveh’s confidence by recalling another powerful city whose defenses did not save it.

keyVerses.text: There is no healing your wound, for your injury is fatal. All who hear the report of you clap their hands over you, for who hasn’t felt your endless cruelty?
keyVerses.why: The closing verse gives the final verdict and explains the reaction of others as a response to Assyria’s widespread cruelty.

themes: public shame of a personified city

questions.question: Who is the “bloody city”?
questions.answer: The city is Nineveh, the Assyrian capital named in verse 7. Calling it bloody accuses it of violence; the accompanying charges name lies, robbery, and predatory gain. These are the poem’s accusations against imperial conduct, not an inherited ethnic description of everyone connected with Assyria.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin with so much sound and motion?
questions.answer: Verses 2-3 stack the whip, wheels, horses, chariots, sword, spear, slain bodies, and corpses. The effect is poetic compression: the reader hears and sees battle in rapid fragments rather than receiving a step-by-step military report.

questions.question: What does “prostitution” mean in this accusation?
questions.answer: Verse 4 portrays the city as an alluring prostitute and mistress of witchcraft who sells nations and families. The image presents Nineveh’s power as seductive, manipulative, and destructive. It is a metaphor about the city’s political influence, not a biography of one woman.

questions.question: How should readers handle the exposure imagery in verses 5-6?
questions.answer: The text presents Yahweh threatening the personified city with forced sexual exposure, filth, and public spectacle. The image reverses the power of the city accused of exploiting nations, while using the humiliation of a female body to do so. Readers differ over how to weigh that reversal and its disturbing means. Its political function does not erase the sexual violence or make it a model for treating women, captives, or civilians.

questions.question: Who is No-Amon, and why is that city mentioned?
questions.answer: No-Amon is Thebes in Egypt, whose sack by Assyria in 663 BCE supplies the historical comparison. Verses 8–10 recall its waters, allies, captivity, the killing of children, and the enslavement of leaders: strong defenses did not prevent catastrophe. Douay-Rheims names Alexandria at 3:8; that edition difference does not make Alexandria and Thebes interchangeable. The example warns Nineveh against trusting its own defenses, without making the depicted atrocities instructions to imitate.

questions.question: What is the force of the commands to draw water and strengthen the fortresses?
questions.answer: Verse 14 sounds like practical siege preparation: gather water, strengthen fortresses, work clay and mortar, and make the brick kiln strong. But verse 15 immediately says fire and sword will devour the city. The commands therefore carry an ironic edge: preparation is described, but it will not change the announced outcome.

questions.question: Why compare merchants, guards, and officials to grasshoppers and locusts?
questions.answer: Verses 15-17 use insects to picture multiplication and sudden disappearance. The merchants are numerous, but the grasshopper strips and flees; the guards and officials settle like locusts on a cold day, then vanish when the sun appears. The image turns abundance into instability.

questions.question: Why do listeners clap at news of the fatal wound?
questions.answer: The closing address to Assyria’s king depicts an incurable wound and a scattered people whose leaders have failed. The final question explains the clapping by asking who has not suffered his endless cruelty. The poem presents the reaction as relief at oppressive power ending, rather than a general instruction to delight in others’ suffering.

questions.question: Why does verse 13 compare the troops to women?
questions.answer: The verse uses a gendered taunt to portray the city’s defenses as vulnerable. Its rhetoric draws on an ancient association of women with weakness in battle, followed by images of open gates and burned bars. Explaining that insult does not endorse the idea that women are inferior or turn the comparison into a factual description of the troops.

glossary.def: The chapter’s opening label for Nineveh, accusing it of bloodshed and violence.
Goods or victims taken by force; in verse 1 it names the city’s predatory gain.
Thebes in Egypt, used in verses 8–10 as a warning that strong defenses and allies cannot guarantee safety.
A military encirclement or attack on a city; verse 14 tells the city to prepare water and strengthen defenses for it.
An insect image used in verses 15-16 for multiplying, stripping, and fleeing.
In verse 17, an image for guards and officials who settle briefly and then disappear.
